title: Played dead, flew free
hookLine: the caged parrot copies it, is thrown out of the cage, and flies (Masnavi 1)

lines: A GIFT THAT BECAME A CAGE.
cards: Plenty of people have a version of themselves they perform. The funny one at parties. The one who's always fine.

The high achiever, the helper, the cool one who doesn't care. Maybe it started as a gift, and people loved it. Then slowly it became a cage, because now you have to keep performing, or they won't love you anymore.
The merchant is home. His parrot has asked what happened in India. Ashamed, he tells it: a wild parrot heard your greeting, trembled, and fell down dead.

teach.b: As soon as the merchant finishes, his own parrot begins to tremble. It shakes in the cage, falls from its perch, and lies there, stiff and still. The merchant is shattered.

He cries out, tears his clothes, and mourns his sweet-voiced bird, the companion of his days; Rumi gives him a long, aching lament. Then, heartbroken, he opens the cage, lifts the little body out, and lets it drop.
And the parrot flies, straight up to a high branch, alive and free. What just happened? the stunned merchant calls. The parrot explains.
That wild parrot in India wasn't dead.

teach.h: YOUR CHARM PUT YOU IN THE CAGE.
teach.b: It was sending me advice by what it did: your beautiful voice, your charm, the way you delight everyone, that's what put you in the cage. Let it go. Become as if dead, and you'll be set free.
The parrot says a kind goodbye to its master, and flies away. Rumi's lesson: the thing that makes people admire you can be the very thing that traps you.

Sufis have a saying for this, which they attribute to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: die before you die. Hadith scholars say it isn't found in the recognized collections, though Sufi teachers treasure it.
It doesn't mean harming yourself in any way.

teach.h: LET THE PERFORMING SELF FALL STILL.
teach.b: It means letting the grasping, performing self fall still, the ego from the lion inside, so that something truer can live. The parrot didn't stop being a parrot. It stopped performing, and it flew.

how: Sufi teachers often read the merchant and the parrot as a lesson in fana, the passing away of the ego, and quote the saying 'die before you die' in explaining it.

o: faking an illness to get out of work
giving up and refusing to try again
letting the performing self fall still

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: gave advice by what it did
what put it in the cage

s: the wild parrot in India really died
it was playing dead, sending advice by its action: let your charm go, and be freed.
the parrot says its beautiful voice is what caged it
the charm that delighted everyone was the thing that trapped it.
die before you die is in the major hadith collections
Sufis attribute it to the Prophet and treasure it, but hadith scholars say it isn't found in the recognized collections.

games.q: you're the caged parrot. you've just heard that a wild parrot fell down dead at your greeting. what do you do?
o: sing louder so your master will free you.
games.why: the parrot understands the lesson in the fall. it plays dead, is thrown out of the cage, and flies to a high branch.

practice: Ask: what do I do mostly so people will like me, or see me a certain way? Always upbeat, always with an answer, pretending not to care; pick one.
Imagine letting it go still, not dramatically, just not doing it, and notice what's underneath; it may be tender, and that's all right.

wordCard.voice: Played dead. The caged parrot copies the wild one, falls still, is thrown out of its cage, and flies free: letting the performing self go. Today's word.
